item.title: Technical SEO on My Own Portfolio: How to Inspect It
item.description: I ran the same technical-SEO checklist I use for clients on my own site: semantic HTML, one h1 per page, JSON-LD Person + FAQ schema, canonical URLs, Open Graph, sitemap and robots. Here is the checklist, and how you can verify each item.
item.content:encoded:
Every week I tell clients the same thing: technical SEO isn't about hacks, it's about removing friction between a crawler and the words you want it to understand. This site is my laboratory — it runs the exact same checklist, and you can inspect every box I ticked by opening the developer tools.

1. One semantic outline per page

A page should read like a document: a single h1, then h2s, then h3s — never skipping levels. My headings follow that tree so Google and AI crawlers can map the page structure.

<h1>Vamshidhar Reddy | Digital Marketing Specialist</h1>
  <h2>Skills</h2>
    <h3>Paid Media / PPC 95%</h3>

2. Structured data (JSON-LD)

Schema tells engines who the page is about before they read a word. This site ships a Person snippet and an FAQPage snippet. You can test them in the Rich Results Test or check the raw JSON in view-source.

3. canonical, sitemap and robots

A canonical URL stops duplicate-content confusion; sitemap.xml tells crawlers what URLs exist; robots.txt controls access. All three live at /sitemap.xml and /robots.txt.

4. Answer-engine ready

The old keyword game is being joined by answer engines. So the same facts live in the FAQ markup and the FAQPage schema, my llms.txt, and the AI chat's knowledge base — consistent entity data is what modern ranking rewards.

SEO now reads like a conversation: give one source, give it clean structure, and let every engine quote you correctly.

The real browser open on this page and press F12 — you'll find all of the above.

item.title: Creative Predictor: My AI That Predicts Ad Performance Before You Spend
item.description: I built Creative Predictor because in paid media, the version of the ad wins. Paste a creative and it predicts its CTR, engagement and conversion using Groq Llama 3.3, OpenAI and HuggingFace — with 20+ modules for quality score, A/B testing, competitor decoding and landing-page analysis.
item.content:encoded:
In paid media, the difference between a good month and a great one is rarely the best ad idea in the room — it's knowing which idea is best before you burn budget finding out. Testing every variant is expensive. Guessing is worse. I built Creative Predictor to take the guess out of it: paste an ad, get a prediction before you spend a rupee.

The core question: which creative wins?

More ad spend doesn't fix a weak creative. A strong hook and a clear angle do. But you can't A/B test fifty variants at real volume. So the value lives in a fast, cheap signal: given this headline, image, offer and angle, how likely is it to click and convert?

What it does

You paste a creative — ad copy, or the whole creative concept — and Creative Predictor returns a predicted CTR, engagement and conversion score. That's the headline feature, and it sits alongside 20+ modules, including quality-score guidance, an A/B testing builder, a competitor decoder, and a landing-page analyzer.

  • Predicted CTR, engagement and conversion for any pasted creative
  • Quality-score guidance to keep costs down
  • A/B test builder for faster iteration
  • Competitor decoder to see what the winners in your niche are doing
  • Landing-page analyzer so the click goes to a page that converts

The problem is the creative, not the budget

The word I keep using in my audits is friction. A creative that scores low on predicted CTR usually has an obvious cause — a vague hook, a claim too good to be believed, no reason to click. Predicting it before you pay for clicks is what separates a paid-media operator from someone who just uploads ads.

The least known secret of paid media: a mediocre creative can cost you more than a great budget.

The engine under the hood

Creative Predictor is currently versioned v13.0, and it's assembled around open models: Groq's Llama 3.3 for raw generation speed, OpenAI for nuanced judgement, and HuggingFace embeddings to compare your ad against the patterns of winners. It proves the point behind my whole portfolio — a marketer who can run testing where engineers are usually brought in.

I wrote the strategy, the metrics and the copy; I built the model, the API and the UI. This is one product of three, all shipped solo — try it and drop in your own ad to see what Creative Predictor predicts for you.

item.title: Pricing a Growth SaaS You Built Solo
item.description: Hook AI is a marketing copy engine I built, launched and charged for solo. Pricing a product when you are the marketer, builder and founder is a different game — here is the thinking: value first, anchoring, packaging, and the one number that actually moves revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Most pricing advice is written for teams: product does X, sales negotiate, finance debates the discount ladder, marketing runs the value metric. When you build the product yourself, there is no debate — there is just you, the maths, and the customers who keep paying or leave. Hook AI taught me that. It's a marketing copy engine I designed, built, shipped and charged for solo, and the pricing felt harder than the code. Here is how I think about it.

Price the outcome, not the hours

The temptation is to price by effort: "I built this in X weeks, so it should cost Y." That's backwards. Buyers never see your hours — they see what the tool replaces. Hook AI writes conversion-ready hooks, headlines and ad copy across 15+ niches, and it bundles its own SEO program, email flows and A/B hero testing. That replaces work a marketer would otherwise bill. Price what it saves, not what it took to write.

Let the middle plan do the selling

Three tiers is a cliché for a reason. A cheap one anchors low, an expensive one makes the middle feel reasonable, and the middle is where most people land. When you build solo, the temptation is to drain everything into the cheapest plan to grow users fast. Users feel great, revenue doesn't. Keep the mid tier the one you actually want to sell.

Ship a demo that feels insultingly generous

Validation beats arguments. Before paying, people need a taste. A free, generous demo — one they'd feel guilty not paying for — does more than a landing page of screenshots. Reveal the value, then price the free experience appropriately.

You aren't selling code. You're selling saved hours and conversations you no longer lose.

Chase the metric a founder actually feels

Vanity metrics flatter — traffic, sign-ups, DAU — feel good but don't pay rent. The number I actually watch is revenue-per-visitor and the conversion rate at which free becomes paid. If a big marketing push lifts visits but the ratio doesn't move, you're attracting tyre-kickers, not customers.

Pricing is a live experiment

Don't set it once. Ship a version, watch the ratio, then nudge. Perhaps the hardest part of building solo is being both the person who wants to please every user and the one who keeps the product alive. The answer to both is the same: charge enough that the free users feel pampered and the paid users feel it was cheap.

The full success story and the real numbers will land here as the product grows. In the meantime — same one rule I give every client: price the outcome, anchor honestly, and track one real number.

item.title: Hook AI: The Copy Engine I Built to Write Conversion-Ready Hooks
item.description: Hook AI is a marketing copy engine I built and launched solo: conversion-ready hooks, headlines and ad copy across 15+ niches, with its own SEO program, email flows and A/B hero testing. Built on Next.js, Supabase, TypeScript, Razorpay and Groq.
item.content:encoded:
Copy is the highest-leverage part of marketing. A hook decides whether an ad gets read, a headline decides whether it gets clicked, and an offer decides whether it gets bought. The catch is that none of it works from one attempt — you need volume of angles, then testing. That's the job I built Hook AI to do.

The job is never one good ad

Clients ask for "an ad". The reality is you need dozens of hooks and headlines per campaign, across different niches, before the data tells you which angle wins. Writing that volume by hand is slow and inconsistent. So I made an engine that generates it at scale and stays on-brand.

What it ships

Hook AI is a Marketing Copy Engine that writes conversion-ready hooks, headlines and ad copy across 15+ niches. It doesn't stop at copy — it bundles its own full SEO program to build topical authority around the content, email flows to keep leads moving, and A/B hero testing so the winning variation surfaces instead of guessing.

  • Hooks, headlines and ad copy across 15+ niches
  • Built-in SEO program around generated content
  • Email flows for nurture and reactivation
  • A/B hero testing to pick the winner with data

Built like a product, not a prompt

It's a real SaaS with payments, not a chat wrapper. Next.js for the app, Supabase for the data, TypeScript for the code, Razorpay for billing, and Groq for fast generation — deployed on Vercel. You can pick a niche and get usable output immediately.

The best hook in the world can't save an ad nobody reads — but the right hook makes the read inevitable.

Why this matters for how I work

Hook AI is proof of the one thing that separates me from a lot of marketers: I don't just plan the strategy, I build the tool that executes it. Strategy, design, build, launch and growth — the full cycle, solo. Try the live engine and generate a few hooks for your own niche here.

item.title: AI Growth Strategy Generator: A Marketing Plan in Minutes, Not Weeks
item.description: Most strategy docs die in a deck. I built the AI Growth Strategy Generator so a business can turn industry, budget and KPI targets into a personalized, budget-optimized marketing plan with effort-vs-impact scoring — in minutes, not weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Most marketing strategies die in a presentation. They get approved, then they live in a PDF nobody reopens, because nothing connects the strategy to a budget, a target, and the order in which to act. The AI Growth Strategy Generator exists to close that gap: answer a short wizard and get a plan you can actually execute.

The inputs

The tool asks for what every growth plan needs and nothing more: the industry, the monthly budget, and the KPI targets that matter — like target CPA and target ROAS. No essays, no blank page, no consultant hand-waving.

The output

From those inputs it builds a personalized, budget-optimized marketing plan, with every channel scored by effort-versus-impact. That last part matters most: it tells you not just what to do, but what to do first given your specific budget.

  • Personalized plan from industry, budget and KPI targets
  • Budget-optimized allocation across channels
  • Effort-versus-impact scoring to set the sequence
  • Built as a guided wizard — no blank canvas

Why a wizard beats a template

A two-lakh budget and a fifty-lakh budget are different businesses. Templates ignore that. The generator does the arithmetic of budget and target — CPA and ROAS expectations — and returns a plan scaled to what you actually have, which is the difference between strategy and decoration.

Strategy is just a budget, a target, and the order of operations.

The point

It's the same muscle I use for clients: take a vague goal, force it through a budget and a target, and output an executable sequence. The generator packages that as a tool you can use on your own — try the wizard here.

item.title: Case Study: How a Paid Media Restructure Cut Cost-Per-Lead 30% and Lifted ROAS to 5.5x
item.description: A client account that had quietly degraded: cost-per-lead creeping toward Rs.1,100, ROAS parked at 3.2x. By consolidating 40+ ad groups, moving to target-CPA bidding and A/B testing creatives, cost-per-lead fell to Rs.770 and ROAS reached 5.5x. Here is exactly what changed.
item.content:encoded:
This is the kind of account every media buyer has met: a lot of ads running, a rising cost-per-lead, and a ROAS that stopped improving months ago. The client wanted cheaper leads and more revenue — not a lecture. Here's the work.

The starting point

Cost-per-lead sat around Rs.1,100 and ROAS was parked at 3.2x. The account had grown without a clean-up: over 40 ad groups, overlapping keywords competing against each other, no consistent bidding strategy, and creatives that had never been properly split-tested.

What was actually wrong

Three problems, none of them unique. First, too many tiny ad groups meant the budget was scattered and the bidding algorithm had no data to optimise. Second, without a target-based bid, the machine chased volume instead of qualified leads. Third, heroes were guesses — a headline with no A/B data is not a decision, it's a hope wearing a budget.

The fix, in order

  • Consolidated 40+ ad groups into tight, themed structures so budget aligned with intent
  • Moved to target-based bidding so the algorithm had a single number to optimise for
  • Started A/B testing creatives and shifted spend to the winner instead of splitting evenly

The result

Cost-per-lead dropped from Rs.1,100 to Rs.770 — roughly a 30% reduction — and ROAS lifted from 3.2x to 5.5x on the same budget. Across the wider program the work also contributed around 15% organic traffic growth and over 70 qualified leads a month.

More budget doesn't fix a broken account. Structure does.

The takeaway

The lessons are boring and powerful: consolidate so the data is clear, bid toward the target you actually care about, and test creatives instead of guessing. It's the same logic I bring to SEO and CRO — remove friction, give the machine a target, and let the numbers decide. If you've got an account that's plateaued, let's talk.

item.title: Case Study: Lifting Organic Traffic ~15% While Paid Media Held the Line
item.description: At Autozilla Software Solutions I own the whole growth mix, so organic and paid had to work as one. This is the organic side: a technical-SEO pass, a content audit, and measuring the +15% traffic growth that groups carried — with the exact checklist I use on any site.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies run SEO and paid media as two separate budgets with two separate agendas. When you own both, you stop treating them as rivals and start treating them as one growth engine: paid buys the test data, organic spends it on durable rankings. That's the setup at Autozilla Software Solutions, where I've been a Digital Marketing Specialist since May 2023. This is the organic half of the story — the same checklist I publish, applied to a real business.

Start with the technical layer

Before any content, the site had to be crawlable and structured. The audit covered exactly the items this portfolio itself demonstrates: one semantic h1 per page, no skipped heading levels, JSON-LD person and FAQ schema, canonical URLs, a live sitemap and robots.txt, and Open Graph tags. Each fix is friction removed between a crawler and the words we want ranked.

Then a content audit — not more volume

More blog posts don't fix a toxic keyword profile. The audit was about subtraction as much as creation: find thin pages, consolidate the cannibalized ones, refresh the pages that had ranking data behind them but stale copy, and only then publish new content where search demand existed and competitors were weak.

The numbers

Within the programme at Autozilla, organic traffic grew by roughly 15%. No single tactic did it — it was the compounding effect of clean technical foundations plus content that answers real queries, measured month over month in the analytics. The same period also ran 70+ qualified leads a month and Rs.2L+ in monthly ad spend, because organic and paid were pointing at the same funnel.

Paid buys the test, organic buys the win. They only work when they're one game plan.

The part that does not publish

Anyone can claim +15%. What makes the number believable is that it drops in alongside a live account with leads and budget — and that the same techniques are demonstrated in public on my own portfolio, crawlable by any engineer who opens the source or checks /sitemap.xml. If you want the same audit run on your site, get in touch.
